title: Opinions of the State Council on Deepening the Implementation of the "AI Plus" Initiative (国务院关于深入实施“人工智能+”行动的意见)
authors: State Council of the People's Republic of China
verification: State Council English-language overview of the guideline read at gov.cn 2026-11-05; the guideline document itself (Chinese full text) not read. Overview reports the six focus areas and 2027/2030/2035 targets.
relevance: The State Council's August 2025 "AI Plus" opinion directs AI adoption across six areas: science and technology, industrial development, consumption upgrades, people's well-being, governance and global cooperation. It sets measurable targets: penetration of new-generation intelligent terminals and AI agents above 70% by 2027 and above 90% by 2030, with China entering a stage of intelligent economy and intelligent society by 2035. A non-binding planning document that anchors China's adoption-first AI policy and complements the TC260 safety-governance framework.

title: Plano Brasileiro de Inteligência Artificial (PBIA) 2024-2028
authors: Ministério da Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (MCTI), with technical support from CGEE
verification: Metadata only (lead): gov.br MCTI page CAPTCHA-gated on 2026-11-05; PBIA overview (launch at the 5th National Conference on Science, Technology and Innovation, R$ 23 billion over four years, public-sector focus, planned high-performance supercomputer) read on the NIC.br-hosted observatory page obia.nic.br/indicadores-pbia 2026-11-05; the plan document itself not read.
relevance: Brazil's AI plan is the executive implementation vehicle for its national AI policy, allocating about R$ 23 billion over 2024-2028 toward public services, infrastructure and a planned high-performance supercomputer for large-data processing and advanced AI algorithms. Launched in July 2024 at the 5th CNCTI and handed to President Lula; NIC.br runs indicator tracking for it. This is the investment programme, distinct from the legislative PL 2338/2024 bill.

title: Política Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (updated policy and Plan de Acción)
authors: Ministerio de Ciencia, Tecnología, Conocimiento e Innovación (MinCiencia)
verification: MinCiencia official policy page read 2026-11-05; the page displays no explicit publication date — it states the first policy was published in 2021, the governance-and-ethics pillar was updated starting 2023, and an "Informe de Resultados 2024" is downloadable. Policy PDFs linked but not opened. May 2024 month is per UNESCO's launch report, not shown at origin.
relevance: Chile's ten-year national AI policy (2021) was updated after generative AI's rapid advance, revising the governance-and-ethics pillar through an online public consultation. MinCiencia credits the policy with creating CENIA, Chile ranking first regionally on the Latin American AI Index (CENIA, 2023), and the first AI doctorate in Chile and Latin America. Three pillars: enabling factors, development and adoption, governance and ethics, operationalized by a Plan de Acción. A strategic framework rather than binding law.

title: Estrategia Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial del Uruguay 2024-2030
authors: AGESIC (Agencia de Gobierno Electrónico y Sociedad de la Información y del Conocimiento)
verification: AGESIC publication page read 2026-11-05; page states the strategy is the "piedra angular" (cornerstone) of public AI policy, developed through a participatory process with technical cooperation from CAF and UNESCO; full PDF linked but not read.
relevance: Uruguay's national AI strategy, published November 2024 after a public consultation, frames AI policy across three thematic axes: governance, AI capabilities, and sustainable development, aiming at inclusive growth, environmental sustainability and national sovereignty. AGESIC leads implementation and monitoring. In 2025 Uruguay became the first Latin American country to adhere to the Council of Europe's AI framework convention, aligning with this strategy. A reference framework, not binding law.

title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS)
authors: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy (FMCIDE), with the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR)
verification: FMCIDE initiative page read 2026-11-05; it describes the co-creation method (1,349 Nigeria-affiliated AI publications from Lens data merged with the global top-50,000 AI journal articles per year 2018-2023, yielding ~1.2 million author-level observations) and states the ministry is co-creating the strategy. No strategy pillars or final PDF on the page; final strategy document dated September 2025 circulates via mirrors but was not read.
relevance: Nigeria's AI strategy aims to steer AI toward job creation, social inclusion and sustainable development, built on a distinctive diaspora-researcher identification method using publication data. The ministry cites AI's projected global economic impact (PwC's US$15.7 trillion by 2030) and Africa's opportunity (IFC's US$234 billion by 2030). The page records the process stage; the co-creation workshop ran in April 2024 and a finalised strategy document followed in 2025.

title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework (Towards the Development of South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy)
authors: Department of Communications and Digital Technologies (DCDT), Republic of South Africa
verification: Framework PDF (20 pages, cover dated October 2024) downloaded and the cover, table of contents and introduction read 2026-11-05; copy is a mirror hosted by africadataprotection.org because the DCDT origin page has a broken TLS certificate for this fetcher. Public inputs were invited by 29 November 2024.
relevance: The framework is the declared first step toward South Africa's national AI policy, applying a futures approach (push of the present, pull of the future, weight of the past) and setting nine strategic pillars spanning talent development, digital infrastructure, R&D and innovation, public-sector implementation, ethical AI guidelines, privacy, safety and security, transparency and explainability, and fairness and bias mitigation. It is a draft framework rather than binding law, and a fuller national AI policy has been developed through subsequent processes.

title: The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
authors: UAE Artificial Intelligence Office (approved by the UAE Cabinet; portal maintained by the Ministry of Cabinet Affairs)
verification: UAE legislation portal policy page read 2026-11-05 (issued 10 June 2024; twelve principles and expected outcomes listed); the full charter document linked on the page was not read.
relevance: The charter lists twelve principles for AI development and use in the UAE — from strengthening human-machine ties, safety and addressing algorithmic bias to data privacy, transparency, human oversight, governance and accountability, and commitment to treaties and applicable laws. It targets public and private sectors, developers, researchers and educational institutions, and is a voluntary policy charter rather than binding legislation, serving the strategic goals of the UAE's national AI strategy.

title: Law on the Digital Technology Industry No. 71/2025/QH15 (Luật Công nghiệp công nghệ số)
authors: National Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (passed 14 June 2025, signed by Chairman Tran Thanh Man)
verification: LuatVietnam full English translation of Articles 1-51 read 2026-11-05 (effective 1 January 2026, with Articles 11, 28 and 29 from 1 July 2025; AI provisions in Chapter IV, Articles 41-45). The Vietnamese official gazette text not read.
relevance: Vietnam's first standalone law on the digital technology industry covers semiconductors, AI and digital assets. Binding AI provisions include human-centred principles (transparency, accountability, explainability, systems must not exceed human control), definitions of high-risk and large-impact AI systems, duties for developers, providers and users, disclosure that an interactive system is AI, and identification marks on AI-generated products. It also bundles semiconductor investment incentives, regulatory sandboxes and tax exemptions for digital talent — notable as hard law from a Global South legislature rather than a voluntary framework.

title: National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE)
authors: Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation (MOSTI) / National AI Office (NAIO, AI Malaysia Berhad)
institution: Government of Malaysia / National AI Office (Digital Ministry)
verification: ai.gov.my governance page read 2026-11-05: AIGE is described as a voluntary guideline with the 7 Key Principles of AI, alongside a voluntary AI Code of Ethics (AICE), a boardroom primer, MY-AI standards gateway, and a 2025 public-sector AI guideline by Jabatan Digital Negara; NAIO's mandate and the "AI Nation 2030" vision are stated. Guidelines PDF not opened; the September 2024 launch date is per accompanying sources, not shown on the page.
relevance: Malaysia's voluntary guidelines set seven principles for responsible and ethical AI and sit within the National AI Office's mandate to lead, coordinate and accelerate the AI ecosystem toward the "AI Nation 2030" vision. The portal also lists a voluntary AI Code of Ethics acting as an operational bridge from the principles to design, development and deployment, plus a 2025 public-sector AI adaptation guideline. Not legally binding; complements the ASEAN-level AI governance guides.

title: White Paper: Regulation and Responsible Adoption of AI for Africa Towards Achievement of AU Agenda 2063
authors: African Union High-Level Panel on Emerging Technologies (APET) and its Secretariat at AUDA-NEPAD, with African AI experts
verification: nepad.org origin returned 403 on 2026-11-05; the executive summary and sections 1-2.7 (background, economic case, Agenda 2063, use cases, challenges, priority areas) read via Dig.Watch's full-text reproduction of the AUDA-NEPAD white paper, which dates the document June 2023. Full PDF not opened.
relevance: The white paper feeding the AU Continental AI Strategy sets dual objectives of promoting AI uptake while addressing risks, aligned to AU Agenda 2063 and STISA-2024. Recommendations include national AI strategies, human capital and education reform, an African AI Research Institute (AAIRI), and an African Union AI Fund of roughly US$100 million over five years (70% to early-stage/scale-up start-ups, 30% to research). It documents Africa's low readiness (3.49/10 on the 2021 Government AI Readiness Index) and highlights African-language NLP (e.g. Masakhane) and gender inclusion. Advisory, not binding.

title: Africa Just AI
authors: Research ICT Africa (Just AI Framework of Inquiry by Pria Chetty and Araba Sey, 10 October 2025; RIA team)
institution: Research ICT Africa, Cape Town, South Africa
verification: RIA project page read in full 2026-11-05, including the Just AI Framework of Inquiry description, funders (IDRC/AI4D, FCDO, and GRTD), timeline February 2021 - January 2026, and the 2023-2026 output list.
relevance: RIA's flagship programme argues African AI governance must be grounded in justice across the entire AI value chain — data, labour, energy, procurement — rather than the ethics-and-safety frame dominating global debates, noting Africa supplies data and labour to AI value chains with little say in benefit distribution. The Framework of Inquiry sets nine inquiries spanning human rights, structural inequality, democratic accountability, economic and data justice, inclusion and sustainability. Outputs include policy briefs on governing AI-enabled surveillance, procurement as a justice failure excluding African SMEs, and a map of national AI strategies in Africa. Research and policy-engagement programme, not binding rules.

title: State of Internet Freedom in Africa 2025: Navigating the Implications of AI on Digital Democracy in Africa
authors: Collaboration on International ICT Policy for East and Southern Africa (CIPESA)
verification: CIPESA launch post of 29 September 2025 read 2026-11-05, including the 14-country coverage, key findings and recommendations, and the report PDF URL (the PDF itself not opened); launch reported at FIFAfrica25 in Windhoek, Namibia.
relevance: CIPESA's annual report surveys AI and digital democracy across 14 African countries (Cameroon, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Tunisia, Uganda, Zimbabwe) and finds none of them has AI-specific legislation, while existing data protection, cybercrime and copyright laws are inadequate for AI harms. It documents AI-enabled surveillance, deepfakes around elections (South Africa 2024, Kenya, Namibia) and bias against low-resource African languages, and recommends AI-specific legislation, mandatory human rights impact assessments and empowered governance institutions. Evidence-based civil-society research, not law.

title: BharatGen
authors: BharatGen Technology Foundation anchored at IIT Bombay (consortium of 9 institutions), backed by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and IndiaAI
verification: BharatGen homepage read 2026-11-05 (model families Param, Shrutam, Sooktam, Patram; launch October 2024 in New Delhi; DST and IndiaAI backing; open weights on Hugging Face and AIKosh; Param2 17B reasoning model featured February 2026). Linked model cards and papers not opened.
relevance: BharatGen is India's government-backed multimodal LLM initiative, building open-weight text, speech and vision models covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages (speech in 12 languages) with data and research built "from the ground up" in India. The homepage reports a 17-billion-parameter Param2 reasoning model, 241,000+ Hugging Face downloads, open benchmarks (BhashaBench, ParamBench) and deployments in hospitals, media and state government. A not-for-profit foundation (Section 8) at IIT Bombay, it exemplifies sovereignty-oriented Global South model building funded by DST/IndiaAI.

title: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (人工智能安全治理框架 2.0版)
authors: National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity (TC260/全国网络安全标准化技术委员会), developed under CAC guidance and led by CNCERT with research institutions and industry
verification: CAC news announcement read 2026-11-05: released 15 September 2025 at the main forum of the 2025 National Cybersecurity Awareness Week; version 1.0 dated September 2024; 2.0 "continuously tracks evolving risks, refines the risk classification, and explores risk grading" (page's own phrasing, translated). Framework PDF linked on the page but not read; v1.0's 13+13 risk taxonomy per the announcement's recollection of coverage.
relevance: China's national cybersecurity standardization committee updated its AI Safety Governance Framework, refining the risk taxonomy inherited from version 1.0 (13 inherent and 13 application risks with 39 technical response measures) and beginning to explore risk grading, with dynamically updated prevention and governance measures. CNCERT frames it as balancing innovation with governance to build a safe, trustworthy and controllable AI ecosystem, implementing the Global AI Governance Initiative. A voluntary technical document rather than a statute, but it signals the direction of Chinese AI regulation.

title: MOFCOM Announcement No. 61 of 2025 on Export Controls over Certain Rare Earth Items (商务部公告2025年第61号)
authors: Ministry of Commerce of the People's Republic of China, Bureau of Security and Control (安全与管制局)
verification: Full Chinese announcement text read at origin 2026-11-05, including scope clauses, licensing denials and the semiconductor end-use review provision; companion Announcement No. 62 of 2025 (rare earth technologies) referenced but not read.
relevance: China's extraterritorial export controls require foreign organisations and individuals to obtain Chinese dual-use licences before exporting to any country items containing 0.1% or more by value of Chinese-origin rare earth items (Annex 1), or produced abroad using Chinese rare earth mining, smelting/separation, metal smelting, magnet-making or recycling technology. Licences are in principle denied for military end-uses, and exports for uses involving logic chips of 14nm or below, memory of 256 layers or above, related semiconductor equipment and materials, or AI with potential military use are reviewed case by case. Binding regulation under China's Export Control Law and Dual-Use Items Regulations, with humanitarian carve-outs; clauses (一) and (二) took effect 1 December 2025, and some measures were later suspended after the November 2025 US-China trade talks.

title: Amendment to Article 10-2 of the Statute for Industrial Innovation (the "Taiwan Chips Act")
authors: Legislative Yuan (Taiwan), passed 7 January 2023; requirements summarised by Lee and Li, Attorneys-at-Law
institution: Government of Taiwan (Legislative Yuan; implemented via Ministry of Finance regulations)
verification: Lee and Li legal analysis of the amendment read in full 2026-11-05 (fetched via reader proxy; law.moj.gov.tw and the law-firm pages block direct automated fetch, so the statute text itself was not read at origin).
relevance: Taiwan's January 2023 amendment provides a 25% investment tax credit for forward-looking innovative R&D expenditures and a 5% credit for purchases of machinery and equipment used in advanced manufacturing processes, effective 1 January 2023 through 31 December 2029. Eligibility is deliberately narrow: applicants must be companies conducting technological innovation within Taiwan, occupy a key position in the international supply chain, meet R&D expense and intensity thresholds and a statutory minimum effective tax rate, and have no serious environmental, labour or food-safety violations in the past three years. Binding tax law that keeps advanced semiconductor capacity onshore in direct response to the US CHIPS Act and EU Chips Act subsidies.

title: National AI Strategy Policy Directions (announced at the inaugural National AI Committee meeting, including the National AI Computing Center plan)
authors: Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT); meeting chaired by President Yoon Suk Yeol
institution: Government of the Republic of Korea / MSIT
verification: MSIT English press release read in full 2026-11-05 (KRW 2 trillion AI Computing Center, GPU expansion to over two exaflops by 2030, KRW 65 trillion private AI investment 2024-2027, AI Safety Institute launching November 2024, Framework Act on AI mentioned). Attachments (Korean and English PDFs) not opened.
relevance: Korea's National AI Committee set policy directions to become one of the world's top-three AI powers, centred on a public-private National AI Computing Center valued at up to KRW 2 trillion and expansion of national GPU capacity to over two exaflops by 2030 (15 times current levels), explicitly supporting domestic AI chips (NPUs, PIMs) and low-interest loans for private AI infrastructure through 2027. Four flagship projects span computing infrastructure, private investment, AI+X adoption across industry and the public sector, and AI safety (an AI Safety Institute plus the Framework Act on AI). A policy-direction document rather than binding law, but the compute-centre plan was subsequently formalised and construction later began in Haenam.

title: ASEAN Framework for Integrated Semiconductor Supply Chain (AFISS)
authors: ASEAN (document prepared for AEM endorsement; hosted by ERIA, which served as knowledge partner per ERIA publications)
verification: AFISS document (16 pages, 2025 "For endorsement" version, 22 September filename) opened and the context, vision, objectives, three focus areas and six strategic thrusts read 2026-11-05 via reader proxy.
relevance: AFISS is ASEAN's flagship strategy for positioning the bloc at the centre of global semiconductor value chains, citing industry growth from US$600 billion (2024) to over US$980 billion (2029) and aiming to transform ASEAN from a back-end assembly/test provider into a vertically integrated semiconductor production base. Six strategic thrusts cover infrastructure quality and resilience, technology innovation/transfer/sharing, supply chain hubs and clusters, industrial and trade policies, market access and connectivity, and talent development and mobility. Explicitly built on non-binding principles and a mapping exercise of member states' complementary strengths; prepared for endorsement by ASEAN economic ministers.

title: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
authors: G7 (Japan presidency, 2023)
institution: G7 / document hosted by Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs
verification: Code of Conduct PDF (8 pages) read in full at origin 2026-11-05 via reader proxy, including the framing (voluntary, risk-based, living document building on the OECD AI Principles) and the risk list (CBRN, offensive cyber, self-replication, democratic values).
relevance: The G7 code sets voluntary, risk-based actions for organizations developing the most advanced AI systems, including foundation and generative models: lifecycle testing (evaluations, red-teaming, secure environments), traceability of datasets and decisions, transparency, incident reporting and internal governance. It explicitly names risks such as CBRN uplift, offensive cyber capabilities, models copying themselves or training other models, and threats to democratic values. Non-binding and applicable across the AI lifecycle; the G7 committed to develop monitoring tools with the OECD and GPAI, and the OECD launched a monitoring framework in February 2025.

title: Resolution A/RES/78/265: Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development
authors: United Nations General Assembly (78th session; draft A/78/L.49, adopted without reference to a Main Committee)
verification: Adopted resolution text (A/RES/78/265, 8 pages) read 2026-11-05 via the Veritas Zimbabwe mirror PDF (docs.un.org viewer did not render text for this fetcher); preamble and operative sections on urgency, interoperable safeguards and digital divides read. US introduction and 120+ co-sponsorship per UN records/secondary coverage, not visible in the text pages read.
relevance: The first UNGA resolution on AI recognizes the urgency of achieving global consensus on safe, secure and trustworthy AI and stresses facilitating inclusive international cooperation to formulate internationally interoperable safeguards, practices and standards that promote innovation and prevent fragmentation of AI governance. It also recognizes existing AI and digital divides and varying levels of technological development between and within countries. Non-binding but near-universal, it primed the capacity-building agenda later carried into the Global Digital Compact.

title: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet
authors: AI Action Summit, Paris (adopted 11 February 2025; signatory list includes about 60 countries plus the African Union Commission and the European Union)
verification: Élysée statement page read 2026-11-05: priorities, deliverables (Public Interest AI Platform and Incubator, IEA observatory on AI energy impact, labour-market observatories, Global Dialogue, Independent International Scientific Panel) and the signatory list were read; the page does not name co-chairs — France-India co-hosting and US/UK non-signature are per summit coverage, not stated on the page. India, Chile, Kenya, Morocco and Nigeria appear as founding members of the Public Interest AI initiative.
relevance: The Paris AI Action Summit statement commits signatories to promoting AI accessibility to reduce digital divides, ensuring AI is open, inclusive, transparent, ethical, safe, secure and trustworthy, fostering innovation while avoiding market concentration, and making AI sustainable for people and the planet. It announces a Public Interest AI Platform and Incubator, an IEA observatory on AI's energy impact, a network of observatories on AI's labour-market effects, and support for a Global Dialogue on AI governance and an independent international scientific panel under the UN Global Digital Compact. A political declaration rather than law; its broad Global South signatory list distinguishes it from earlier G7-led processes, while the US and UK declined to sign.

title: Guidance for generative AI in education and research
authors: Fengchun Miao and Wayne Holmes (UNESCO)
verification: UNESCO publication (48 pages, © UNESCO 2023, ISBN 978-92-3-100612-8) opened and the front matter plus short summary read 2026-11-05 via the UCL Discovery open-access mirror; unesco.org article page returned 403 and unesdoc.unesco.org shows a cookie wall, so the origin pages did not render for this fetcher. Authors per the mirror's file record and UNESCO's article metadata.
relevance: UNESCO's first global guidance on generative AI in education states that publicly available GenAI tools are emerging faster than national regulatory frameworks can adapt, leaving user data privacy unprotected and educational institutions unprepared to validate the tools. It aims to support countries to implement immediate actions, plan long-term policies and develop human capacity to ensure a human-centred vision of these technologies. Soft guidance for ministries rather than binding rules, distributed through UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of AI infrastructure and widely taken up by Global South education systems.
